input: What is a Stack in Data Structures?
output: A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle. Elements are inserted (push) and removed (pop) from only one end, called the top of the stack.
ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. These properties ensure reliable transaction processing in a database.

input: What is a Deadlock in Operating Systems?
output: A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting for another resource acquired by some other process.
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is a connection-oriented protocol that ensures reliable data transfer between devices over a network.

input: What is a Queue? Explain its types.
output: A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In First Out (FIFO) principle. Types include simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, and double-ended queue (deque).
B-Trees are self-balancing search trees designed for systems that read and write large blocks of data, like databases and file systems.
Normalization is the process of organizing data in a database to avoid redundancy and ensure data integrity. It involves decomposing a table into smaller tables without losing data.

The 3-Tier Architecture includes the Presentation Tier (user interface), Application Tier (business logic), and Data Tier (database). It separates concerns to allow better scalability and maintainability.

input: What is the difference between process and thread?
output: A process is an independent program in execution, while a thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. Threads share the same memory space; processes do not.

Paging is a memory management scheme that eliminates the need for contiguous memory allocation. Physical memory is divided into fixed-size blocks called frames and logical memory into blocks of the same size called pages.
DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-friendly domain names like www.example.com into IP addresses that computers use to identify each other on the network.

input: Explain OSI Model in Computer Networks.
output: The OSI model is a conceptual framework used to understand network interactions in seven layers: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, and Application.
A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data so that operations like access, insertion, deletion, and updating can be performed efficiently.

input: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?
output: An array stores elements in contiguous memory locations and supports direct access. A linked list stores elements (nodes) that contain data and a reference to the next node, allowing dynamic memory allocation.
A stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last In First Out (LIFO) principle. Insertion and deletion happen from only one end called the top.

input: What are real-life examples of a stack?
output: Examples include a pile of plates, undo feature in editors, and browser history.

input: What operations are performed on a stack?
output: The main operations are push (add element), pop (remove element), peek (view top element), and isEmpty (check if stack is empty).
A queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In First Out (FIFO) principle. Elements are inserted at the rear and removed from the front.
Types of queues include simple queue, circular queue, priority queue, and double-ended queue (deque).
A linked list is a linear data structure where each element is a node containing data and a reference (link) to the next node.

input: What are types of linked lists?
output: Types of linked lists are singly linked list, doubly linked list, and circular linked list.
A binary tree is a tree data structure where each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.

input: What is a binary search tree (BST)?
output: A binary search tree is a binary tree where for each node, values in the left subtree are smaller and values in the right subtree are larger.
Tree traversal refers to visiting all nodes of a tree systematically. Common traversals are inorder, preorder, and postorder.

input: What is the difference between BFS and DFS?
output: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores neighbors level by level, using a queue. Depth-First Search (DFS) explores as far as possible along a branch before backtracking, using a stack or recursion.
A graph is a collection of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections between nodes). It can be directed or undirected.
An adjacency matrix is a 2D array used to represent a graph, where each cell (i,j) indicates if there is an edge between vertex i and vertex j.
An adjacency list represents a graph as a collection of lists, where each vertex has a list of connected vertices.
Hashing is the process of mapping data to a fixed-size value (hash) using a hash function. It is used for fast data retrieval.
A hash table is a data structure that stores key-value pairs and uses hashing to calculate an index into an array of buckets.
A collision occurs when two keys hash to the same index. Techniques like chaining and open addressing are used to handle collisions.
A heap is a complete binary tree that satisfies the heap property: in a max heap, parent nodes are greater than child nodes; in a min heap, parent nodes are smaller.
A priority queue is a special queue where each element has a priority, and elements are served based on priority, not just order of insertion.
A trie is a tree-like data structure used to store strings efficiently, especially useful for prefix-based searching like autocomplete.
Dynamic programming is an optimization technique where subproblems are solved and stored to avoid recomputation.
Memoization is a technique of storing the results of expensive function calls and returning the cached result when the same inputs occur again.
Recursion is a process where a function calls itself directly or indirectly to solve a problem.
Time complexity measures the amount of time an algorithm takes as a function of the input size.
Space complexity measures the amount of memory space an algorithm uses relative to the input size.
Big O notation describes the worst-case time or space complexity of an algorithm, helping to analyze its performance.

input: What is the time complexity of searching in a binary search tree?
output: The average time complexity is O(log n), but in the worst case (unbalanced tree) it can be O(n).

input: What is the time complexity of binary search on a sorted array?
output: The time complexity is O(log n) because the array is divided by 2 at each step.
